highlights.title: Highlights
highlights.description:
Conway's refinement conjecture [LM24, Conj. 1.1.1(2)] says: if $ab=cd$ for omnific integers, then $a=ef$, $b=gh$, $c=eg$, $d=fh$ for some omnific integers $e,f,g,h$. In an integral domain this is the same as saying that every element is primal. Conway normal form identifies the omnific integers with a ring of generalised power series, $\mathbb Z+\mathbb R((\mathbf{No}^{<0}))_\kappa$. The guide proves that every element of this ring is primal. It proves the same for $Z+R((G^{<0}))_\kappa$ under conditions on $G$ that include (A1)--(A3) of [LM24, Thm. 9.0.1]. There are four ideas.

Germs. Let $K$ be a field of characteristic zero and $G$ a Cauchy-complete ordered abelian group. Let $J$ be the ideal of series in $K((G^{\le0}))$ whose support is bounded away from $0$. The germ of $b$ at $\gamma$ is the class of $b^{|\gamma}=t^{-\gamma}b_{|\gamma}$ modulo $J$ [Ber00, Def. 6.1]. Germs obey Berarducci's convolution formula [Ber00, Lem. 7.5]. The Cantor--Bendixson rank of $0$ in the closed support drops along germs just below $0$.

Transcendence. Germs that are new at a given rank are transcendental over the germs already present. Adjoining them one at a time shows that $K((G^{\le0}))/J$ is a polynomial ring over $K$. So $J$ is prime; for $G=\mathbb R$ this is [Ber00, Cor. 9.8]. The same method shows that $K((\mathbb R^{\le0}))$ is a polynomial ring over the series with finite support. So $K((\mathbb R^{\le0}))$ is a GCD domain.

Reduction along Archimedean classes. Grouping exponents along a convex subgroup gives a $D+M$ construction. Primality then reduces to two smaller problems. At the leading Archimedean class the exponents become real, and the GCD theorem applies. At a limit of classes, primality of germs and an induction on the classes finish the proof.

Surreal exponents. Conway's construction of a number between two small sets gives the cofinality and completeness that the reduction needs. Conway normal form takes the result back to the omnific integers.

phases.title: Two primality criteria
phases.description:
This chapter proves two general lemmas about primal elements. Both are used in the reduction along Archimedean classes.

The first is about a $D+M$ construction. Let $\pi:A\to L$ be a homomorphism of $L$-algebras and $S$ a subring of $L$. An element of $\pi^{-1}(S)$ is primal there if it is primal in $A$ and its image is primal in $S$. If its image is $0$, we need instead that $L$ is the fraction field of $S$.

The second deduces primality in a domain $T$ from primality in a quotient $T/J$. It uses ring endomorphisms that kill $J$ and preserve divisibility. Later, $T/J$ is a ring of germs and the endomorphisms restrict supports to Archimedean balls.

phases.title: Germs of translated truncations
phases.description:
Let $K$ be a field, $G$ a nontrivial ordered abelian group, and $J$ the ideal of series in $K((G^{\le0}))$ whose support is bounded away from $0$. The germ of $b$ at $\gamma$ is the class of the translated truncation $b^{|\gamma}=t^{-\gamma}b_{|\gamma}$ modulo $J$ [Ber00, Def. 6.1].

This chapter proves the facts about germs that the next chapter needs. If $G$ is Cauchy complete, germs obey Berarducci's convolution formula. The germs of $b^{|\gamma}$ are the germs of $b$, shifted by $\gamma$. The germ of $b$ at $\gamma$ is nonzero exactly when $\gamma$ is in the closure of the support. It is a constant exactly when the germs just below $\gamma$ vanish.

Inductions use the Cantor--Bendixson rank of $0$ in the closed support. It depends only on the germ. If the germ is not a constant, the rank drops along the germs just below $0$.

phases.title: Polynomial presentations
phases.description:
First the facts from the previous chapter are stated as axioms on germ maps. Let $S$ be a subalgebra of germs such that each element of $S$ is the germ of a series with all its germs in $S$. Let $X$ be a series whose germs below $0$ lie in $S$, but whose germ $x$ does not. Then $ax\notin S$ for every nonzero $a\in S$. If $S$ is a domain, then $x$ is transcendental over $S$. The proof takes a relation of least degree and applies the germ maps to it. Characteristic zero reduces it to degree one.

Adjoining such germs one at a time shows that $K((G^{\le0}))/J$ is a polynomial ring over $K$ when $G$ is Cauchy complete. So $J$ is prime. The same holds for series with support of cardinality less than $\kappa$.

For real exponents, a series has only constant germs exactly when its support is finite. The same method then shows that $K((\mathbb R^{\le0}))$ is a polynomial ring over its subring of series with finite support. That subring is a GCD domain [LM24, Fact 2.5.2]. By Gauss's lemma, $K((\mathbb R^{\le0}))$ is a GCD domain too.

phases.title: Reduction along Archimedean classes
phases.description:
Let $Z$ be a pre-Schreier subring of a field $R$ of characteristic zero. This chapter proves that every element of $Z+R((G^{<0}))_\kappa$ is primal under conditions on $G$.

Let $C$ be a convex subspace of $G$. Grouping exponents along $C$ turns $Z+R((G^{<0}))_\kappa$ into a $D+M$ construction. Here $D=Z+R((C^{<0}))_\kappa$ and $M$ consists of series over $R((C))_\kappa$ with negative exponents in $G/C$. By the first criterion, a series is primal if its regrouping is primal and its restriction to $C$ is primal.

The proof is an induction on the Archimedean classes met by the support. If there are finitely many, take $C$ below the leading class. The regrouped series then has real exponents, so it is primal by the GCD theorem. If there are infinitely many, take $C$ below a limit of classes. If $G/C$ is Cauchy complete, every germ is primal, and the second criterion applies.

The chapter ends with a converse: the refinement property forces $R$ to be the fraction field of $Z$.

phases.title: Surreal numbers and omnific integers
phases.description:
This chapter checks the conditions of the general theorem for surreal exponents.

Each Archimedean complement in $\mathbf{No}$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb R$. Conway's construction of a number between two small sets gives the needed cofinalities. It also fills small cuts. A cut criterion turns this into Cauchy completeness of the quotients of $\mathbf{No}$.

So every element of $\mathbb Z+\mathbb R((\mathbf{No}^{<0}))_\kappa$ is primal. Conway normal form identifies this ring with the omnific integers. Hence the omnific integers have the refinement property, and every irreducible omnific integer is prime.
